title: Thermometer Reader
context: Grade 5, the pages on temperature. An adult sees a thermometer read. What the pages are doing is asking children to read scales whose small marks are not all worth the same, so the one habit that matters is finding what one small mark is worth before reading.

writeup.why: Say what temperature is and what measures it, know the chapter's landmark readings on both scales, find what one small mark is worth, and read a thermometer by counting marks.
writeup.look: A tall thermometer with a green liquid column, labels up its scale and small marks between them, and on one phase a second scale beside it marked only at four readings.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Thermometer Reader' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of gaps or marks counted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The thermometer stands upright at x 480, y 220, a tube 60 wide and 470 tall with its bulb at the bottom, its tube, marks and labels in near-black ink and its liquid column green, labelled Reading. On the first phase a shelf runs along y 640 from x 700 to x 1100 with a bowl of ice, cups of water and a cup of tea on it, and the thermometer is dragged into each; the cups can then be dragged into a row along y 560, coldest at the left. On the second phase the Celsius scale runs up the left of the tube, and the other scale, violet, labelled Other scale, stands on the right with only four marks; the four landmark buttons, freezing water, room temperature, body temperature and boiling water, stand in a column at x 760, y 260. On the third phase a tapped label is deep blue, labelled Given, each gap between two neighbouring labels lights amber as it is counted, and the worth of one small mark is pinned beside the scale at x 600 in vermilion, labelled One mark. On the fourth the marks above the label below the column light one at a time as they are counted. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and a deg C key and a deg F key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last thermometer stays up, with the worth of one small mark pinned beside it and the reading in green.

phases.win: the cups line up from coldest to hottest, each with its column height beside it
phases.does: dips the thermometer into each and puts them in order from coldest to hottest
phases.goal: temperature is how hot or cold something is, and a thermometer measures it
phases.says: Dip it in. Does the column go up or down?
phases.check: Away from the screen: which is hotter, a cup of milk just heated or a glass of milk from the fridge?

writeup.delight: On the second phase, when the boiling water landmark is tapped, a few small bubbles rise inside the drawn cup beside the tube as the column climbs to the top label.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet read. On the first phase the thermometer stands beside a shelf with a bowl of ice, cups of water and a cup of tea. On the second it stands with the Celsius scale on the left, the other scale on the right marked at four readings, and four landmark buttons below. On the third a scale stands with its labels and small marks and no column yet. On the fourth the column stops between two labels. One thing moves, once: the thermometer, the first landmark button, or the lowest label gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.

observations.why: the liquid in the tube takes up more room when it is warmer.
observations.soWhat: the height of the column shows how hot or cold something is, which is its temperature.
observations.observe: The column rose in the tea and sank in the ice water.

observations.why: the two scales measure the same temperature with different numbers.
observations.soWhat: always say which scale a reading is on, deg C or deg F.
observations.observe: The same landmark sat at two different numbers on the two sides of the tube.

observations.why: what one small mark is worth depends on the labels and on how many steps lie between them.
observations.soWhat: find what one small mark is worth before reading any thermometer.
observations.observe: On one thermometer a small mark was worth one degree, and on another it was worth more.

observations.why: the marks sit between the steps, like fence posts between gaps.
observations.soWhat: count the steps, not the marks, when finding what one small mark is worth.
observations.observe: There was always one more step than there were small marks between two labels.

source_tool.description: A tall thermometer stands in the working area, its tube and marks in near-black ink and its liquid column green, labelled Reading. On the first phase cups of water, a bowl of ice and a cup of tea sit on a shelf, and the child drags the thermometer into each; the column rises or falls and the cups are ordered from coldest to hottest. On the second phase the Celsius scale runs up the left of the tube and a second scale, violet, labelled Other scale, stands on the right with only four marks: four landmark buttons, freezing water, room temperature, body temperature and boiling water, set the column at those four printed readings. On the third phase the child taps two neighbouring labels, each gap between them lights amber as it is counted, and the worth of one small mark is typed and pinned beside the scale in vermilion, labelled One mark. On the fourth the column stops between labels, and the marks above the label below it light as they are counted. The labels a question gives are deep blue, labelled Given. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the gaps or marks counted.
source_tool.art_direction: Cups of water on a kitchen shelf / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: What is one small mark worth here? Count the steps between two labels.
voice.onNext: A new thermometer. Look at its labels first.
voice.onFinish: You found what one small mark was worth, and read the column.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Dip the thermometer anywhere and read it.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: What one small mark is worth

placement.where: After the class has put a classroom thermometer into a cup of cool water and a cup of warm water and read both. The tool is what lights each gap and each mark as it is counted, which a printed thermometer cannot.

answer_key.rule: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is, and a thermometer measures it. On the Celsius scale water freezes at 0 deg C and boils at 100 deg C. Water boils at 100 deg C, which is 212 deg F. Normal body temperature is about 37 deg C, which is about 98.6 deg F. Before reading a scale, find what one small mark is worth: the gap between two neighbouring labels, divided by the number of steps between them, which is one more than the number of small marks. Then count the marks from the label below the column and add.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the reading the child typed and draws the column at that reading beside the real one, so the two tops are seen apart. The gaps between the two labels light again one at a time, and the worth of one small mark is shown beside them. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Temperature is how hot or cold something is.
Put the thermometer in the tea: its column rises high.
Put it in the ice water: its column falls low. So the tea is hotter.
items.answer: The tea is hotter. A thermometer measures how hot or cold each one is, which is its temperature.
items.question: A cup of tea and a glass of ice water sit on a table. Which is hotter, and what measures how hot each one is?
items.checkpoint: A thermometer measures temperature, how hot or cold something is.
items.misconception: Thinking a thermometer tells how much water is in the glass, because its column goes up and down like a level.

steps: On the Celsius scale, water boils at 100 deg C.
On the Fahrenheit scale, the same boiling water reads 212 deg F.
They are two readings of one temperature, on two scales.
So water boils at 100 deg C, which is 212 deg F.
items.answer: Water boils at 100 deg C, which is 212 deg F.
items.question: At what temperature does water boil on the Celsius scale, and what is that on the Fahrenheit scale?
items.checkpoint: Water boils at 100 deg C, which is 212 deg F: one temperature on two scales.
items.misconception: Thinking the Fahrenheit reading is the hotter one because its number is bigger, when the two readings are the same temperature.

steps: From one label to the next is 10 degrees.
The 4 small marks cut that gap into 5 equal steps.
So one small mark is worth 2 degrees on this thermometer.
items.question: A thermometer is labelled 60, 70 and 80 deg C, with 4 small marks between neighbouring labels. What is one small mark worth?
items.checkpoint: Find what one small mark is worth: the gap between two labels, divided by the number of steps between them.
items.misconception: Counting the 4 marks as 4 steps, when 4 marks cut the gap into 5 steps, which gives two and a half degrees a step.

steps: One small mark is worth 2 degrees here.
Start at the label below the column: 60 + 6 = 66.
So the thermometer reads 66 deg C.
items.question: On a thermometer labelled 60, 70 and 80 deg C, one small mark is worth 2 degrees. The column stops 3 small marks above the 60 label. What does it read?
items.checkpoint: Find what one small mark is worth, then count the marks up from the label below the column.
items.misconception: Taking each mark as one degree without checking, and so reading 63 deg C.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: What does a thermometer measure?
items.final_answer: Temperature: how hot or cold something is

items.question: At what temperature does water freeze on the Fahrenheit scale?
Labels 20 and 25 deg C have 4 small marks between them. What is one small mark worth?
On a thermometer where one small mark is worth 1 degree, the column stops 3 marks above the 25 label. What is the reading?
What is normal body temperature on the Celsius scale?
Labels 40 and 60 deg C have 4 small marks between them. What is one small mark worth?
Labels 30 and 50 deg C have 4 small marks between them. The column stops 2 marks above the 30 label. What is the reading?
items.final_answer: 38 deg C, because each mark is worth 4 degrees

items.question: Two cups of water are at 45 deg C and 70 deg C. Which is hotter, and by how many degrees?
items.final_answer: The cup at 70 deg C, by 25 degrees

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: dips the thermometer into a cup or thing on the first phase
set the column at one of the four printed readings
picks two neighbouring labels and lights the gaps between them
lights the small marks above a label as they are counted
types the worth of one small mark or a reading

teaching_notes: Before anyone reads a scale, find what one small mark is worth: count the steps between two labels, which is one more than the number of small marks. Different thermometers have different marks, so check each one. Use only the four readings the chapter pairs on the two scales; it gives no rule for changing scales, and the tool gives none. Room temperature is 21 deg C, which is 69.8 deg F. Celsius and Fahrenheit are the names of the two scales.
